definitionEn: A dynamic virtual replica of a physical object, building, or urban system continuously updated with live sensor data.
meaningVi: bản sao số mô phỏng theo thời gian thực một đối tượng
existingExample: Civil engineers construct a digital twin of an ageing bridge to simulate extreme wind loads before approving structural repairs.

definitionEn: Relating to technologies that simulate the sense of touch through controlled forces, vibrations, or physical motion.
meaningVi: thuộc xúc giác, tạo cảm giác rung chạm mô phỏng
existingExample: Advanced haptic gloves enable trainee surgeons to feel realistic tissue resistance during virtual-reality operating simulations.

definitionEn: Hardware and software platforms capable of perceiving environments and executing complex tasks with minimal human intervention.
meaningVi: hệ thống tự hành có khả năng tự quyết định
existingExample: Establishing clear legal liability remains a major obstacle before autonomous systems can safely manage urban airspace.

definitionEn: The use of statistical algorithms and machine learning on historical datasets to forecast future outcomes or behaviours.
meaningVi: phân tích dự báo xu hướng từ dữ liệu lịch sử
existingExample: Power utilities apply predictive analytics to anticipate seasonal demand spikes and prevent cascading regional blackouts.

definitionEn: The legal rule that digital data falls under the privacy laws of the nation where it is collected.
meaningVi: chủ quyền dữ liệu thuộc phạm vi pháp lý quốc gia
existingExample: Heightened concerns over data sovereignty have prompted several nations to require cloud providers to store citizen records domestically.

definitionEn: The technical removal or encryption of personally identifiable attributes from datasets so individuals cannot be traced.
meaningVi: quy trình ẩn danh hóa dữ liệu nhằm bảo vệ danh tính
existingExample: Strict data anonymisation allows university epidemiologists to share hospital records globally without breaching patient confidentiality.

definitionEn: Openness regarding the data inputs, logic, and evaluation criteria used by automated decision-making systems.
meaningVi: tính minh bạch trong cách thức thuật toán ra quyết định
existingExample: Civil liberties advocates insist on algorithmic transparency whenever automated software screens job applicants or credit requests.

definitionEn: A complex computational system whose internal reasoning process is opaque and difficult for human auditors to interpret.
meaningVi: mô hình hộp đen khó giải thích logic xử lý bên trong
existingExample: Regulators are understandably reluctant to approve an unaccountable black-box model for high-stakes clinical triage decisions.

definitionEn: Characterised by governance or problem-solving driven primarily by technical specialists and engineering efficiency.
existingExample: A purely technocratic vision of smart cities often overlooks grassroots community needs in favour of flashy sensor networks.

definitionEn: The theory that technological progress autonomously shapes cultural norms, economic structures, and historical change.
meaningVi: thuyết quyết định luận công nghệ
existingExample: Sociologists critique simplistic technological determinism by demonstrating how public policy actively steers how innovations are adopted.

definitionEn: A hypothetical future point when self-improving artificial intelligence surpasses human intellect, causing unpredictable societal shifts.
meaningVi: điểm kỳ dị công nghệ khi AI vượt xa trí tuệ người
existingExample: While futurists debate the feasibility of a technological singularity, ethicists urge immediate focus on present-day AI governance.

definitionEn: Relating to feedback-driven control systems or the functional integration of electronic machinery with biological organisms.
meaningVi: thuộc điều khiển học; tích hợp máy móc và sinh học
existingExample: Modern cybernetic prosthetics translate subtle nerve impulses into fluid hand movements for upper-limb amputees.

definitionEn: A solid material whose electrical conductivity can be precisely controlled, forming the physical foundation of modern microchips.
meaningVi: vật liệu bán dẫn hoặc linh kiện vi mạch cốt lõi
existingExample: Global automotive production ground to a halt when pandemic bottlenecks disrupted specialised semiconductor fabrication plants.

definitionEn: An integrated electronic circuit containing the core arithmetic and control logic required to execute computer instructions.
meaningVi: bộ vi xử lý trung tâm trên một vi mạch tích hợp
existingExample: Miniaturising the microprocessor enabled everyday household appliances to monitor energy consumption with minimal power draw.

definitionEn: Exclusively owned, controlled, and licensed by a private firm with legal restrictions on external inspection or modification.
meaningVi: thuộc quyền sở hữu độc quyền, mã nguồn đóng
existingExample: Public schools dependent on proprietary software suites often face steep recurring licensing fees whenever budgets tighten.

definitionEn: Freely available online to any reader or developer without subscription barriers or restrictive paywalls.
meaningVi: truy cập mở, miễn phí sử dụng và chia sẻ rộng rãi
existingExample: Releasing satellite climate datasets on an open-access portal accelerated independent flood-mapping efforts across developing regions.

definitionEn: An outdated computing platform or software infrastructure that remains in active use because replacing it is costly or risky.
meaningVi: hệ thống công nghệ cũ lỗi thời nhưng vẫn đang vận hành
existingExample: Migrating national aviation schedules off a decades-old legacy system requires meticulous phased testing to avoid service outages.

definitionEn: Engineered to match human physical anatomy and movement patterns, thereby maximising comfort and preventing strain.
existingExample: Employers investing in ergonomic workstations and adjustable displays witness marked declines in repetitive wrist injuries.

definitionEn: Operating smoothly without bureaucratic delays, technical obstacles, or cumbersome steps for the end user.
meaningVi: liền mạch, mượt mà không gặp trở ngại thao tác
existingExample: Contactless transit gates provide a frictionless commuting experience, encouraging motorists to switch to metropolitan rail.

definitionEn: The integration of game mechanics such as badges, streaks, and challenges into non-game digital platforms to boost engagement.
meaningVi: trò chơi hóa nhằm tăng tương tác và động lực
existingExample: Although gamification keeps language-app learners returning daily, behavioural psychologists warn it can encourage superficial habit loops.

definitionEn: High-fidelity audiovisual and robotic technologies that give remote participants the sensation of being physically present elsewhere.
meaningVi: công nghệ hiện diện từ xa chân thực như đang có mặt
existingExample: Multinational engineering teams increasingly adopt holographic telepresence to curb unnecessary long-haul business flights.

definitionEn: Artificially generated information mirroring statistical properties of real-world records, used to train AI while protecting privacy.
meaningVi: dữ liệu tổng hợp nhân tạo dùng để huấn luyện thuật toán
existingExample: Medical software startups increasingly rely on synthetic data to train diagnostic models without exposing sensitive patient histories.

definitionEn: To make a once-exclusive technology, resource, or creative tool affordable and accessible to the general public.
existingExample: Low-cost cloud servers and open libraries have helped democratise software engineering for entrepreneurs in emerging markets.

definitionEn: To remove or anticipate a difficulty, requirement, or manual step so that it is no longer necessary.
meaningVi: loại bỏ hoàn toàn sự cần thiết của một bước/quy trình
existingExample: Automated biometric passport gates obviate the need for prolonged manual document checks during peak airport arrivals.

definitionEn: a way of life that involves a lot of sitting and little exercise.
existingExample: Office workers who lead a sedentary lifestyle face a higher risk of heart disease.

definitionEn: the condition of being very overweight in a way that is dangerous to health.
existingExample: A tax on sugary drinks could help tackle childhood obesity.

definitionEn: a diet that contains the right amounts of different kinds of food.
existingExample: Maintaining a balanced diet is more effective than following strict diets.

definitionEn: the average number of years a person is expected to live.
existingExample: Improvements in sanitation have dramatically increased life expectancy.

definitionEn: intended to stop something bad from happening.
existingExample: Investing in preventive care is cheaper than treating diseases later.

definitionEn: lasting for a long time or keeping coming back.
existingExample: Diabetes is a chronic condition that requires lifelong management.

definitionEn: a large number of cases of a disease in a community at the same time.
existingExample: Some experts describe smartphone addiction as a modern epidemic.

definitionEn: the state of being healthy, comfortable and happy.
existingExample: Regular exercise improves both physical and mental well-being.

definitionEn: the condition of a person's mind and emotions.
existingExample: Employers are paying more attention to the mental health of their staff.

definitionEn: caused by stress.
existingExample: Stress-related illnesses are a leading cause of absence from work.

definitionEn: the process of getting the food needed for health and growth.
existingExample: Poor nutrition in early childhood can affect brain development.

definitionEn: food that is quick and easy to eat but bad for your health.
existingExample: Banning junk food advertising during children's programmes could reduce obesity.

definitionEn: the way medical services are organised in a country.
existingExample: An ageing population puts enormous pressure on the healthcare system.

definitionEn: unwanted effects of a medicine or treatment.
existingExample: All medicines can cause side effects, so patients should follow their doctor's advice.

definitionEn: giving people a vaccine to protect them against a disease.
existingExample: Mass vaccination programmes have eradicated diseases such as smallpox.

definitionEn: the practice of keeping yourself and your surroundings clean to prevent illness.
existingExample: Good hand hygiene is one of the simplest ways to prevent infection.

definitionEn: easily affected or harmed by something.
meaningVi: dễ bị ảnh hưởng, dễ mắc
existingExample: Elderly people are more susceptible to infections during the winter.

definitionEn: to make pain or a problem less severe.
existingExample: Gentle stretching can alleviate back pain caused by long hours at a desk.

definitionEn: to identify an illness by examining someone.
existingExample: Early detection makes it easier to diagnose and treat cancer.

definitionEn: movement of the body that uses energy, such as walking or sport.
existingExample: Health experts recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity a week for adults.

definitionEn: a population in which the proportion of older people is increasing.
existingExample: Japan faces the challenges of a rapidly ageing population.

definitionEn: a strong need to keep doing or using something harmful.
existingExample: Support groups can help people overcome addiction.

definitionEn: care given to cure an illness or injury.
existingExample: In some countries, many people cannot afford to seek medical treatment.

definitionEn: the sudden start of something unpleasant, especially a disease.
existingExample: Health authorities acted quickly to contain the outbreak.

definitionEn: dealing with the whole person rather than only the symptoms of an illness.
existingExample: A holistic approach to health considers diet, sleep and stress as well as medication.

definitionEn: likely to cause death.
existingExample: Early diagnosis can stop a condition becoming life-threatening.

definitionEn: a disease that cannot be cured and will cause death.
existingExample: Hospices care for people with terminal illnesses.

definitionEn: spread by direct contact.
existingExample: Highly contagious respiratory viruses can spread rapidly across densely populated cities without timely vaccination.

definitionEn: a disease spreading across many countries.
existingExample: The pandemic exposed weaknesses in health systems.

definitionEn: the body's system for fighting infection.
existingExample: Lack of sleep can weaken the immune system.

definitionEn: protection that arises when most of a population is immune.
existingExample: High vaccination rates help achieve herd immunity.

definitionEn: bacteria no longer responding to antibiotics.
existingExample: The overuse of antibiotics fuels antibiotic resistance.

definitionEn: diseases of the heart and blood vessels.
existingExample: Smoking greatly increases the risk of cardiovascular disease.

definitionEn: a disease in which the body cannot control blood sugar.
existingExample: Type 2 diabetes is closely linked to diet and exercise.

definitionEn: high blood pressure.
existingExample: Excessive salt intake can lead to hypertension.

definitionEn: a disease that is not spread between people.
existingExample: Non-communicable diseases such as cancer are now the leading cause of death worldwide.

definitionEn: poor health caused by a lack of food or the right nutrients.
existingExample: Malnutrition stunts children's growth.

definitionEn: not getting enough food to be healthy.
existingExample: Undernourished children struggle to concentrate at school.

definitionEn: the amount of energy consumed from food.
existingExample: Reducing calorie intake is key to losing weight.

definitionEn: food changed by industrial methods.
existingExample: Processed food is often high in salt and sugar.

definitionEn: the amount of food served to one person.
existingExample: Growing portion sizes contribute to weight gain.

definitionEn: a pill or product taken to add nutrients to the diet.
existingExample: Most people with a balanced diet do not need dietary supplements.

definitionEn: not doing enough physical exercise.
existingExample: Physical inactivity is a major risk factor for chronic disease.

definitionEn: exercise that raises the heart rate, such as running.
existingExample: Aerobic exercise strengthens the heart and lungs.

definitionEn: a planned programme of exercise.
existingExample: It is difficult to stick to a strict fitness regime.

definitionEn: the chemical processes that turn food into energy.
existingExample: Metabolism tends to slow down with age.

definitionEn: not getting enough sleep.
existingExample: Chronic sleep deprivation impairs memory.

definitionEn: the inability to sleep.
existingExample: Using screens before bed can worsen insomnia.

definitionEn: a feeling of worry or nervousness.
existingExample: Exam pressure can trigger anxiety in teenagers.

definitionEn: a mental illness causing deep, lasting sadness.
existingExample: Talking therapies can help people with depression.

definitionEn: negative feelings society has about something.
existingExample: Campaigns aim to reduce the stigma surrounding mental illness.

definitionEn: professional help with personal or emotional problems.
existingExample: Schools should provide free counselling for students.

definitionEn: treatment for an illness or psychological problem.
existingExample: Physical therapy helped her recover after the accident.

definitionEn: calmly paying attention to the present moment.
existingExample: Mindfulness can reduce stress and improve concentration.

definitionEn: basic health services such as local doctors.
meaningVi: chăm sóc sức khỏe ban đầu
existingExample: Rural areas often lack adequate primary healthcare.

definitionEn: a doctor who treats general health problems in the community.
existingExample: Patients may wait weeks to see a general practitioner.

definitionEn: a list of people waiting for treatment.
existingExample: Long waiting lists push some patients towards private clinics.

definitionEn: a system that gives everyone access to healthcare.
existingExample: Universal healthcare is funded through taxation in many countries.

definitionEn: medical care that patients pay for themselves.
existingExample: Private healthcare can reduce waiting times but excludes poorer people.

definitionEn: insurance that pays medical costs.
existingExample: Without health insurance, treatment can be very expensive.

definitionEn: not having enough money to operate properly.
existingExample: Underfunded hospitals struggle to retain staff.

definitionEn: having too much work and too few resources.
existingExample: Overstretched nurses are leaving the profession.

definitionEn: a trained person who provides medical care.
existingExample: There is a global shortage of healthcare professionals.

definitionEn: a doctor's written order for medicine.
existingExample: Many antibiotics are only available on prescription.

definitionEn: available without a prescription.
existingExample: Over-the-counter painkillers can be dangerous in large doses.

definitionEn: to take medicine without a doctor's advice.
existingExample: People who self-medicate may hide serious illnesses.

definitionEn: a sign of illness.
existingExample: Many patients ignore early symptoms.

definitionEn: the process of returning to health.
existingExample: She made a full recovery after surgery.

definitionEn: giving body organs to be transplanted.
existingExample: An opt-out system could increase organ donation.

definitionEn: ending a life to relieve suffering.
existingExample: Euthanasia remains illegal in most countries.

definitionEn: the condition of living for an exceptionally long period of time.
existingExample: Diet and strong social ties contribute to longevity.

definitionEn: an inherited tendency to develop a condition.
existingExample: Some people have a genetic predisposition to heart disease.

definitionEn: passed from parents to children.
existingExample: Some forms of deafness are hereditary.

definitionEn: causing harm.
existingExample: Smoking has detrimental effects on almost every organ.

definitionEn: good for your health.
existingExample: Children need wholesome meals to grow properly.

definitionEn: a substance needed for growth and health.
existingExample: Fresh vegetables are rich in essential nutrients.
